title: Reading Augustine's Confessions

objectives.can: Read the opening of the Confessions: prayer addressed to God in the second person, questions, antithesis, and the Psalms woven into the prose.

explanation.summary: The Confessions begins as a prayer. Augustine speaks to God in the second person, asks question after question, sets words against each other, and weaves phrases of the Psalms and of Paul into his own sentences without marking them. This lesson teaches you what to look for and sends you into the first five sections of Book 1.

sections.heading: A book spoken to God
body: Most Latin prose is addressed to a reader. The Confessions is addressed to God. The first words are *Magnus es, domine*: a predicate adjective, a second-person verb and a vocative. From there the book keeps its second person: *tu excitas*, *fecisti nos ad te*, *da mihi*, *dic animae meae*. When you find the subject of a verb in this book, ask first whether it is *tu*, 'you', understood.

The title word *confessio* has two meanings in Christian Latin, and readers have long noticed that Augustine uses both: to acknowledge, as one acknowledges faults, and to praise. In Book 1, section 10, the verb appears in the first person, *Confiteor tibi, domine*. Do not read the title as only 'admission of guilt'.

A note on the text. The edition prints *u* for consonantal *v* (*uirtus*, *inuocare*) and *i* for *j*, and it has a few misprints, one at the start of section 1.3. The analysis in this library is automatic, and some words in these sections are tagged wrongly. The exercises draw only on words with a single certain reading.

sections.heading: The Psalms and Paul inside the sentences
body: Augustine knew the Bible by heart, and his prose is full of its phrases, used as part of his own sentences and not set off in quotation. The table shows some from the first sections. Where the words differ from the Vulgate, remember that Augustine usually read the Bible in an older Latin version than Jerome's, so small differences of wording are expected.
What matters for reading is this: when a phrase sounds like Scripture, it probably is. Look it up. The meaning of the Psalm line often explains the turn Augustine gives it.

head: Augustine
The biblical verse
What he does with it
rows: Psalm 144:3 and Psalm 47:2: *Magnus Dominus, et laudabilis nimis*
Turns a third-person acclamation into a second-person address; *ualde* for *nimis*.
*magna uirtus tua et sapientiae tuae non est numerus*
Psalm 146:5: *Magnus Dominus noster, et magna virtus ejus, et sapientiæ ejus non est numerus*
The same lines, with *tua* and *tuae* for *ejus*.
*quomodo autem inuocabunt, in quem non crediderunt? aut quomodo credent sine praedicante?*
Romans 10:14: *Quomodo ergo invocabunt, in quem non crediderunt? aut quomodo credent ei*
Uses Paul's questions to ask which comes first, calling on God or knowing him.
A promise that he turns into the next step of his own argument.
Quoted inside a question about where God is.
*dic animae meae: salus tua ego sum*
Psalm 34:3: *dic animæ meæ: Salus tua ego sum*
A prayer that God say to his soul what the Psalm says.

sections.heading: Questions as a way of thinking
body: Section 1.1 is a chain of questions. *utrum sit prius inuocare te an laudare te*: a double indirect question, 'whether to call on you comes first or to praise you'. *sed quis te inuocat nesciens te?* 'But who calls on you without knowing you?' *an potius inuocaris, ut sciaris?* 'Or rather are you called on, so that you may be known?' Each question tests an answer and moves to the next. He does not wait for a reply; the questions are part of the prayer.

Section 1.2 turns the questions on place: how can he call on God to come into him, when God made heaven and earth and is already everywhere? *quo enim recedam extra caelum et terram?* The subjunctive *recedam* is deliberative: 'where am I to go?' And *quo te inuoco, cum in te sim?* asks, 'where do I call you to, when I am in you?', with *sim* a subjunctive in a *cum* clause.

Section 1.5 turns the questions into requests. *Quis mihi dabit adquiescere in te?* 'Who will grant me to rest in you?' and *quis dabit mihi, ut uenias in cor meum*: 'who will give me that you come into my heart?' The imperatives that follow, *dic*, *aperi*, *noli abscondere*, make it plain that the questions were prayers.

sections.heading: Balance, antithesis and sound
body: Augustine had been a teacher of rhetoric, and the opening pages are shaped. The famous sentence of 1.1, *quia fecisti nos ad te et inquietum est cor nostrum, donec requiescat in te*, sets *inquietum* against *requiescat* and *ad te* against *in te*: the heart made towards God, and resting in him. *donec* with the subjunctive gives the aim: 'until it rests'.

Section 1.1 also has a matched pair, *quaeram te, domine, inuocans te et inuocem te credens in te*, 'let me seek you by calling on you, and let me call on you believing in you': a verb and *te*, then a participle that says how, twice.

Section 1.4 is a long run of opposites. God is *numquam nouus, numquam uetus*, never new, never old. The sequence goes on in matched pairs and in participles, *mutans omnia ... innouans omnia ... portans et implens et protegens, creans et nutriens*, a row of present participles with no finite verb. The endings echo each other, and so the sequence sounds like a chant. Short antithetical clauses like *amas nec aestuas*, 'you love and do not burn', and *irasceris et tranquillus es*, 'you are angry and are calm', set an ordinary human feeling against its opposite.
None of this needs special training to see. Read the passage aloud, find the verb in each clause, and listen for the repeated words.

sections.heading: A way into the opening
body: Read each section aloud and mark the second-person verbs and the vocatives. Find the questions and say what each one asks. Look for the words that echo a Psalm or a letter of Paul. Then look for the pairs of opposites, and for the long chains of participles. Finally, say what the section does as a whole: praises, asks, or requests.

misunderstandings: Reading *confessio* only as admission of guilt. In Augustine it is also praise.
Treating a phrase that sounds biblical as Augustine's own invention. Much of the language of these pages is Scripture, unmarked.
Taking the questions as requests for information. They are part of the prayer, and many are answered by Scripture a few lines later.
Assuming a Psalm line in Augustine reads exactly as in the Vulgate. He usually used an older Latin Bible, and the wording can differ.

deeper.heading: Why the second person
body: The Confessions tells the story of Augustine's own life, but it tells it to God and so in the second person. This changes how the reader stands: the reader overhears. Readers have long discussed what that does to the book, and the question is open; the Latin shows the fact plainly in its verbs and its vocatives.

examples.analysis: *Magnus es, domine*: *Magnus* is a predicate adjective, *es* a second-person verb and *domine* a vocative, so the sentence is direct address. The echo of the Psalms is clear: see Psalm 146:5. *uirtus* and *numerus* are nominative nouns of the second clause, 'your power is great and of your wisdom there is no number'. Further on, *fecisti* is a second-person perfect, 'you made', and the antithesis of the famous sentence is *cor* ... *inquietum* against *requiescat*, 'until it rests'.

examples.analysis: *nam etsi descendero in infernum, ades* quotes Psalm 138:8: *descendero* is a future perfect, 'even if I go down'. The question *quo te inuoco, cum in te sim?* is a puzzle: *inuoco* is 'I call on', *sim* a subjunctive of *sum* in a *cum* clause, 'when I am in you'. Augustine asks where one can call God to, if one is already in him.

examples.analysis: A list of paradoxes. *numquam nouus, numquam uetus*: two words that are opposites, in matched phrases. *aestuas* and *zelas* are second-person verbs, and *amas nec aestuas* sets love against heat. *irasceris et tranquillus es* does the same with anger and calm. The effect is cumulative: the more opposites, the more the reader sees that God is spoken of without ordinary categories.

examples.analysis: *Quis mihi dabit adquiescere in te?* is a question that is a request. *dabit* is a future, with *mihi* in the dative: 'who will give to me'. Then the imperatives: *dic* is the imperative of *dico*, and it is repeated, *dic mihi ... dic animae meae*. *salus tua ego sum* are the words he asks God to say: 'I am your salvation' (Psalm 34:3).

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: Great is our Lord, and great is his power: and of his wisdom there is no number.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: The Psalm line behind the opening of the Confessions. *Magnus Dominus*: a statement about the Lord, in the third person. Augustine says *Magnus es, domine*, to him. The second half, *et sapientiae ejus non est numerus*, becomes in Augustine *et sapientiae tuae non est numerus*. The same words carry two different relations between speaker and God.

options: God, in the second person: *es* is second-person singular and *domine* is a vocative

practice.explain: *es* is second-person singular, 'you are', and *domine* is the vocative of address. The opening is a prayer.

options: *homo*; *laudare te* is the infinitive that *uult* governs, and *aliqua portio creaturae tuae* is in apposition to *homo*
practice.explain: *homo* is nominative singular, the subject of *uult* ('wants'). *laudare te* is what he wants: 'to praise you'. *aliqua portio creaturae tuae* explains what sort of man it is.

check.prompt: What is *utrum sit prius inuocare te an laudare te*?

quoted.title: Confessions
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: A double indirect question, 'whether to call on you comes first or to praise you', with *sit* in the subjunctive
check.explain: *utrum ... an* sets two alternatives, and the subjunctive *sit* shows an indirect question after *da mihi scire et intellegere*.

check.prompt: *quomodo autem inuocabunt, in quem non crediderunt? aut quomodo credent sine praedicante?* Where do these questions come from?

quoted.title: Confessions
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: From Paul's letter to the Romans (10:14), worked into Augustine's sentence
Augustine made them up, and they have no biblical source
check.explain: The Vulgate of Romans 10:14 has *Quomodo ergo invocabunt, in quem non crediderunt? aut quomodo credent ei*. Augustine uses Paul's questions to ask which comes first, calling on God or knowing him.

check.prompt: In *quaeram te, domine, inuocans te et inuocem te credens in te*, what do the participles *inuocans* and *credens* add?

quoted.title: Confessions
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: A contrast with the main verb
The means or manner: 'by calling on you', 'believing in you'
check.explain: Present participles agreeing with the speaker say how he will seek and call: by calling, believing. The two halves are matched.

check.prompt: *nam etsi descendero in infernum, ades* echoes a Psalm. Which verse, and what is the tense of *descendero*?

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: If I ascend into heaven, thou art there: if I descend into hell, thou art present.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: Psalm 138:8; a future perfect, 'even if I go down'
check.explain: The Vulgate of Psalm 138:8 has *si descendero in infernum, ades*. *descendero* is a future perfect, looking ahead to a completed going-down.

options: A deliberative question: 'where am I to go?'
check.explain: In a direct question, a first-person subjunctive asks what one is to do. The sense is 'where am I to go, outside heaven and earth?'

check.prompt: What figure is *numquam nouus, numquam uetus*?

quoted.title: Confessions
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: An antithesis: two opposite words in matched phrases, a paradox about God
check.explain: *nouus* and *uetus* are opposites. Setting both under *numquam* is a paradox, and 1.4 is built from many such pairs.

check.prompt: How is the run *mutans omnia ... innouans omnia ... portans et implens et protegens, creans et nutriens* built?

quoted.title: Confessions
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: As a list of finite verbs in the future
As a chain of present participles describing God, with no finite verb of their own, echoing each other in sound
check.explain: The participles are in apposition to the vocative addressed to God; they pile up attributes. Their endings in *-ans* and *-ens* echo each other.

check.prompt: In 1.5 Augustine writes *dic animae meae: salus tua ego sum*. Where do these words come from?

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: Bring out the sword, and shut up the way against them that persecute me: say to my soul: I am thy salvation.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: From Psalm 34:3, nearly word for word
They have no source: they are his own
From the Gospel of John, nearly word for word
check.explain: The Vulgate of Psalm 34:3 has *dic animæ meæ: Salus tua ego sum*. The words Augustine asks God to say are the Psalm's own.

reading.reference: Augustine of Hippo, Confessions 1.1 – Augustine of Hippo, Confessions 1.5
reading.why: The opening of the Confessions: the prayer in the second person, the chain of questions, the antitheses of 1.4, and the Psalms woven into the sentences. (The edition has a misprint at the start of section 1.3.)
